1.pericope_label: Balaam abandons enchantments, sets his face toward the wilderness, sees Israel encamped by tribes, and the Spirit of God comes upon him as he takes up his parable

schools.summary: John Gill says Balaam saw that it was good in the Lord's sight, what he approved of and was well-pleasing to him, and that it was his determined mind that Israel should be blessed and not cursed, from which there was no turning him by offering sacrifices to him, and much less by his sorceries and divinations. Gill notes that Balaam lifted up his eyes being on Mount Peor, and that he took up his parable of prophecy, as the Targums render it, his prophetic speech, which with a loud voice he expressed in the hearing of Balak and his nobles. John Calvin says it is evident that Balaam, in order to gratify the wicked king for the sake of the reward, endeavoured by various shifts and expedients to obtain an answer in accordance with his wishes; thus do the wicked seek to propitiate God by delusive means, just as we soothe children by coaxing, and God for some time allowed him to gloat upon his fallacious oracle. He now, however, lays closer constraint upon him, and, breaking off all delay, dictates an answer which he compels him to deliver, Calvin says; for his obedience is not here praised as if, when he understood the will of God, he yielded voluntarily and abandoned his monstrous cupidity, but because now there was no more room for subterfuge, and he dared not stir his foot, as if God had put forth his hand to retain him in his place. When it is said that the Spirit of God came upon him after he turned his eyes toward the wilderness and beheld the camp of Israel, how they were marshalled according to their tribes, we must understand it thus, Calvin says: not that he was influenced by a sincere feeling of good-will, so that the sight itself suggested grounds for blessing, but that he was induced by the inspiration of the same Spirit who afterwards put forth his influence in the prophecy itself. It is said, then, that the Spirit of God was upon him, not as if it had begun to inspire him at that particular moment when he cast his eyes upon the camp of Israel, Calvin says, but because it prompted him to look in that direction, in order that the impulse of prophecy might be stronger in him, as respecting a thing actually before his eyes. But after the Spirit had thus affected his senses, or at any rate had prepared them to be fit instruments for the execution of his office, it then also directed his tongue to prophesy, Calvin says, but in an extraordinary manner, so that a divine majesty shone forth in the sudden change, as if he were transformed into a new man; in a word, the Spirit of God was upon him, showing by manifest token that he was the author of his address, and that he did not speak of his own natural intelligence. To the same intent it is said that he took up his parable, Calvin adds, because the character of his address was marked with unusual grandeur and magnificent brilliancy, in order to touch more closely to the quick those that might hear it. On the preface, Calvin says it has no other object than to prove that he is a true prophet of God, and that he has received the blessing which he pronounces from divine revelation; and indeed his boast was true as regarded this special act, though it might be the case that pride and ambition impelled him thus to vaunt. It is, however, probable that he prefaced his prophecy in this way by the inspiration of the Spirit, in order to demand more credit for what he said, Calvin says, and from a consideration of this purpose we may the better gather the meaning of his words: Balaam dignifies himself with titles by which he may claim for himself the prophetic office, and whatever therefore he predicates of himself we may know to be the attributes of true prophets, whose marks and distinctions he borrows. To this end he says that he is hidden in his eye, by which he means that he does not see in the ordinary manner, but that he is endued with the power of secret vision, Calvin says. Interpreters agree that the word is equivalent to another meaning to close, Calvin reports: thus some render it in the pluperfect tense, the man who had his eyes closed, and this they refer to the blindness of Balaam, since his ass saw more clearly than himself; others, who perceive this gloss to be too poor, expound it as whose eye was open, but since this interpretation too is unnatural, Calvin has no doubt but that he says his eyes were hidden, because in their secret vision they have more than human power. Calvin reports that Jarchi observes that some of the Hebrews have from hence conjectured that Balaam was blind of one eye, and notes that David makes use of the same root to signify hidden things when he says, in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom. Unless, perhaps, we may prefer that he was called the man with hidden eyes as despising all human things, and as one with whom there is no respect of persons, Calvin says, though the former interpretation is the more suitable; and assuredly, when he adds immediately afterwards the hearer of the words of God, which saw the vision of the Almighty, it must be taken expositively. To the same effect is what is added in conclusion, he who falls and his eyes are opened, Calvin says; for the exposition which some give, that his mind was awake whilst he was asleep as regarded his body, is far-fetched, and there is a tameness in the opinion of those who refer it to the previous history where it is recorded that after Balaam had fallen under the ass his eyes were opened to see the angel. Comparing himself, therefore, to the prophets, he says that he fell down in order to receive his visions, Calvin concludes; for we often read that the prophets were prostrated, or lost their strength, and lay almost lifeless, when God revealed himself to them, for thus did it please God to cast down his servants as to the flesh, in order to lift them up above the world, and to empty them of their own strength, in order to replenish them with heavenly virtue.

Matthew Henry says the blessing itself which Balaam here pronounces upon Israel is much the same with the two in the foregoing chapter, but the introduction to it is different, and the method of proceeding varies in several instances. Balaam laid aside the enchantments which he had hitherto depended on, used no spells or charms or magic arts, finding they did him no service, Henry says; it was to no purpose to deal with the devil for a curse when it was plain that God was determined immovably to bless, and sooner or later God will convince men of their folly in seeking after lying vanities which cannot profit, for to what purpose should he seek for enchantment when he knew that God was out of the reach of them. He did not now retire into a solitary place as before, but set his face directly towards the wilderness where Israel lay encamped, Henry says, and since there is no remedy but they must be blessed, he will design nothing else but will submit by compulsion. Now the Spirit of God came upon him, that is, the Spirit of prophecy, as upon Saul to prevent him from taking David, Henry says: he spoke not his own sense, but the language of the Spirit that came upon him. He used a different preface now from what he had used before, much like that of David, yet savouring very much, as some think, of pride and vain-glory, taking all the praise of this prophecy to himself and magnifying himself as one of the cabinet-council of heaven, Henry says. Two things he boasts of: the favour God did him in making known himself to him, for he heard the words of God and saw the vision of the Almighty, God himself having met him and spoken to him, and with this he was greatly puffed up, whereas Paul speaks with humility of his visions and revelations, but Balaam speaks of his with pride. The second is his own power to receive and bear those revelations, Henry says: he fell into a trance indeed, as other prophets did, but he had his eyes open, and this he mentions twice, though the words in the original are not the same, the man whose eyes were shut, as some think it may be read, but now having his eyes open. When he attempted to curse Israel he owns he was in a mistake, but now he began to see his error, and yet still he remained blinded by covetousness and ambition, those foolish and hurtful lusts, Henry says. Those that oppose God and his people will sooner or later be made to see themselves wretchedly deceived, Henry concludes, and many have their eyes open that have not their hearts open, are enlightened but not sanctified; and that knowledge which puffs men up with pride will but serve to light them to hell, whither many go with their eyes open.

Adam Clarke summarises the chapter thus: Balaam, finding that God was determined to bless Israel, seeks no longer for enchantments, and the Spirit of God coming upon him he delivers a most important prophetic parable; Balak's anger is kindled against him and he commands him to depart to his own country; Balaam vindicates his conduct and delivers a prophecy relative to the future destruction of Moab by the Israelites, also of Edom, of the Amalekites and of the Kenites, predicting also the destruction of Asshur and Eber by the naval power of Chittim, which should afterwards be itself destroyed, after which Balaam and Balak separate. On the words he went not, as at other times, to seek for enchantments, Clarke says we have already had occasion to observe that the proper meaning of the word nachash is not easily ascertained; here the plural is rendered enchantments, but it probably means no more than the knowledge of future events, and when Balaam saw that it pleased God to bless Israel he therefore thought it unnecessary to apply for any farther prophetic declarations of God's will as he had done before, for he could safely infer every good to this people from the evident disposition of God towards them. The Spirit of God came upon him, Clarke says: this divine afflatus he had not expected on the present occasion, but God had not yet declared the whole of his will. He took up his parable, that is, his prophetic declaration couched in highly poetic terms and in regular metre, as the preceding were, Clarke says. On the man whose eyes are open, Clarke believes the original shethum should be translated shut, not open, for in the next verse, where the opening of his eyes is mentioned, a widely different word is used, galah, which signifies to open or reveal; at first the eyes of Balaam were shut, and so closely too that he could not see the angel who withstood him, till God opened his eyes, nor could he see the gracious intentions of God towards Israel till the eyes of his understanding were opened by the powers of the Divine Spirit. This therefore he mentions, we may suppose, with humility and gratitude, and to the credit of the prophecy which he is now about to deliver, that the Moabites may receive it as the word of God which must be fulfilled in due season, Clarke says; and his words in their meaning are similar to those of the blind man in the Gospel, once I was blind, but now I see. John Wesley says that at other times means in former times, and that toward the wilderness means where Israel lay encamped, Balaam expecting what God of his own accord would suggest to him concerning this matter. Came upon him means inspired him to speak the following words, Wesley says. On whose eyes are open, Wesley gives the Hebrew as who had his eyes shut, but now open, meaning the eyes of his mind, which God had opened in a peculiar and prophetical manner, whence prophets are called Seers; it implies that before he was blind and stupid, having eyes, but not seeing nor understanding.

Charles Ellicott says that he set his face toward the wilderness means towards the place where the Israelites were encamped on the steppes of Moab, and that abiding in his tents means encamped according to the order prescribed for the respective tribes, the cognate noun being rendered tabernacles later in the chapter. In regard to the two former utterances it is said that Jehovah put a word in the mouth of Balaam, Ellicott says, but in the present case the Spirit of God came upon, or over, him; the same expression is used of the messengers of Saul and of Saul himself, and the prophecy of Caiaphas affords another instance of the sovereign power of the Spirit as displayed through the medium of wicked men. On Balaam the son of Beor hath said, Ellicott says the Hebrew word neum is imperfectly rendered by hath said, being the word which is commonly used in the prophetical books of Scripture to denote a Divine saying, and rarely used when a human author is named; it occurs in the Pentateuch only in Genesis 22, Numbers 14, and in this chapter, where it is found at verses 3 and 4 and again at 15 and 16. On the man whose eyes are open, Ellicott says there is great diversity of opinion respecting the meaning of the word which is here rendered open, and which as it is here written occurs in no other place; if shatham is identified with satham it means to close, not to open. The meaning, however, of this verse is sufficiently explained by that which follows, whichever rendering of the word shethum is adopted, Ellicott says: Balaam appears to have been thrown into an ecstatic state, as was Saul and as were many of the ancient prophets, and whilst the eye of the outer senses was closed, the eye of the inner senses was preternaturally opened. Keil and Delitzsch say that verses 3 and 4 contain the preface to the prophecy, the divine saying of Balaam the son of Beor, the divine saying of the man with closed eye, the divine saying of the hearer of divine words, who sees the vision of the Almighty, falling down and with opened eyes. For the participial noun neum the meaning divine saying, effatum and not inspiratum Domini, is undoubtedly established by the expression the saying of Jehovah, which recurs in Numbers 14 and Genesis 22 and is of constant use in the predictions of the prophets, Keil says; and this applies even to the few passages where a human author is mentioned instead of Jehovah, such as this chapter at verses 3 and 4 and 15 and 16, and also 2 Samuel 23, Proverbs 30, and Psalm 36, where a saying is ascribed to the personified wickedness.

debates: What the word rendered open means: Clarke argues flatly for shut, since the next verse uses galah for opening, and reads it as Balaam's own confession that he had once been unable to see even the angel; Wesley and Keil render it as closed, Wesley expanding it to shut but now open; Henry reports both readings and uses the ambiguity homiletically; Ellicott declines to decide, saying the form occurs nowhere else and that the following verse settles the sense either way; Calvin rejects both the pluperfect closed and the open reading as too poor and unnatural respectively, and proposes a third, that the eyes were hidden, because in their secret vision they have more than human power

Whether Balaam's preface is culpable: Henry hears pride and vain-glory in it, Balaam taking all the praise of the prophecy to himself and magnifying himself as one of the cabinet-council of heaven, where Paul speaks of his visions with humility; Calvin allows pride and ambition may have impelled the vaunt, but holds the preface true as regarded this act and probably prompted by the Spirit itself in order to demand more credit for the prophecy

What ceasing from enchantments shows: Henry and Gill take it as forced submission to a determined God, Henry adding that God will convince men of their folly in seeking after lying vanities; Clarke reduces the stake by arguing that nachash here probably means no more than the knowledge of future events, so that Balaam merely judged further inquiry unnecessary; Calvin makes it neither submission nor prudence but the closing of the last subterfuge, so that he dared not stir his foot

How the Spirit could rest on such a man: Ellicott and Henry both reach for Saul as the parallel, Ellicott adding Caiaphas as an instance of the sovereign power of the Spirit through the medium of wicked men; Calvin insists on the order, that the Spirit prompted the look before the look prompted the blessing, since Balaam felt no sincere good-will at all
outliers: Calvin's image of the wicked propitiating God by delusive means, just as we soothe children by coaxing
Calvin's report from Jarchi that some of the Hebrews conjectured from this verse that Balaam was blind of one eye
Clarke's comparison of Balaam's words to those of the blind man in the Gospel, once I was blind, but now I see
Henry's warning that many have their eyes open who have not their hearts open, being enlightened but not sanctified, and that such knowledge will only light them to hell
Keil's note that the prophetic formula is even ascribed to personified wickedness in the Psalm
Calvin's reading of the falling down as the ordinary posture of prophecy, God casting down his servants as to the flesh in order to lift them above the world
themes: the Spirit on a wicked man

4.pericope_label: The third oracle: Israel goodly in its tents, spread like valleys and gardens, watered from full buckets, its king higher than Agag, brought out of Egypt with the strength of a buffalo, couched as a lion whom none dare rouse

schools.summary: John Gill says Balaam speaks of God speaking to him, which he did several times, and with which he was greatly elated. On how goodly are thy tents, Gill says it is not that the matter of which they were made was so rich, or their structure so admirable, but the order in which they were placed was so beautiful and agreeable. As the valleys are they spread forth means long and broad, lying between several mountains and reaching from hill to hill, Gill says: so the armies of Israel lay encamped in the plains and villages of Moab, making a very considerable length and breadth, the camp of Israel being said to be twelve miles long and twelve miles broad, so the Targum. This may denote the lowness of the saints and people of God in their own eyes, and their largeness in themselves, Gill says, and especially when the place of their tents shall be enlarged and the curtains of their habitations be stretched forth in the latter day; and also their fruitfulness, meads and valleys abounding with herbs and flowers, as the churches of God do with the fruits of the Spirit, grace and righteousness, and with plants of the Lord's right hand planting. Some render it as brooks and torrents of water, so the Targum of Jonathan, which diffuse and spread themselves, and on the banks of which stand beautiful trees in goodly order, Gill notes. He shall pour the water out of his buckets, that is, God shall plentifully send down rain out of the clouds upon these valleys, gardens and trees and make them fruitful, Gill says; and this may be a figure of the grace of God with which his churches are watered, and become fruitful by means of the word and ordinances, which is conveyed through them out of the fulness which is in Christ. On God brought him forth out of Egypt, Gill says Balaam repeats what he had said in a former prophecy, and that he shall eat up the nations his enemies means the seven nations of Canaan, which should be subdued by Israel, and that with as much ease as a lion devours its prey, nor would the Canaanites be able to make any more resistance to them than a creature in the paws of a lion, the phrase denoting their utter destruction. He couched may respect the posture of the armies of Israel in the plains of Moab, Gill says. John Calvin says the internal condition of prosperity enjoyed by the people is described by various similitudes akin to each other and expressive of the same thing: he compares them to valleys and well-watered gardens, and then to trees which were rendered succulent by abundance of moisture, and finally to fields whose seeds imbibe fatness from the waters. The word we translate spread forth some prefer to render streams, and the Hebrew word signifies both, Calvin says, but the course of the metaphors requires that valleys should rather be understood; and for the same reason he has given the translation aloe-trees, for although the word often means tabernacles he has no doubt but that it here refers to trees, so as to correspond with what follows as to the cedars. They are called trees which the Lord hath planted as surpassing the ordinary growth of nature in their peculiar excellency, and exhibiting something more noble than the effect of human labour and skill, Calvin says. In the concluding similitude the interpreters have erred, in Calvin's opinion: some translate it his seed many waters, others on many waters, but the literal translation runs far better, namely that he is like a rich and fertile field whose seed is steeped in much water; thus far Balaam has been speaking of God's blessing, which shall enrich the people with an abundance of all good things. He now begins to enlarge on their outward prosperity, Calvin says, namely that the people of Israel shall be powerful and flourishing and endowed with a warlike spirit to resist the assaults of their enemies, for it would not be sufficient that they should abound with all blessings unless the ability to defend them should also be superadded. It is by no means a probable conjecture that he speaks of Saul, who made prisoner of their king Agag in the battle with the Amalekites, Calvin says, but their opinion is the more correct one who suppose that this was a name common to all the kings of that nation; it was therefore God's intention to declare the superiority of his chosen people to the Amalekites, nor need we be surprised that they should be thus brought into especial antagonism with them, not only because they were the constant enemies of Israel but because their power was then excessively great, as the twentieth verse will show. Although for a long time afterwards there was no king in Israel, still there is no absurdity in the fact that the commonwealth should be designated by that name, and especially since God had postponed the full accomplishment of his grace until the time of the establishment of the kingdom, Calvin says; hence, in this prophecy, Balaam, however little he might have been aware of it, embraced the time of David, and consequently he predicted things which were only accomplished in Christ, on whom the adoption was founded. On the blessing and cursing, Calvin says this mode of expression signifies that the Israelites were elected by God on these terms, that he would account as conferred upon himself whatever injury or benefit they might receive; nor is there anything new in this, that God should declare that he would be an enemy to the enemies of his Church and, on the other hand, a friend to her friends, which is a token of the high favour with which he regards her. Hence we are taught that whatever good offices are performed towards the Church are conferred upon God himself, who will recompense them faithfully, Calvin says, and at the same time that believers cannot be injured without his avenging them, even as he says, he that toucheth you toucheth the apple of my eye. If any should object that Balaam himself went unrewarded although he blessed the people, the reply is an easy one, Calvin says, that he was unworthy of any praise, who was by no means disposed in the people's favour of his own accord and out of pure and generous feeling, but who was forcibly drawn in a direction whither he was unwilling to go; meanwhile this point remains unshaken, that whosoever have contributed their labours for the Church's welfare, and have been her faithful helpers, shall be sure partakers of the blessing which is here promised.

Adam Clarke says there is no indication in the Hebrew that Balaam fell into a trance, these words being added by our translators and not in the original: nophel is the only word used, and simply signifies falling, or falling down, perhaps in this instance by way of religious prostration. On lign aloes which the Lord hath planted, Clarke says it may be rendered as the tents which the Lord hath pitched, for it is the same word which is used in the fifth verse; but from other parts of Scripture we find that the word also signifies a species of tree, called by some the sandal tree and by others the lignum or wood aloes. This tree is described as being eight or ten feet high, with very large leaves growing at the top, Clarke says, and it is supposed that a forest of those at some distance must bear some resemblance to a numerous encampment; as the word comes from a root which signifies to spread or branch out, and is therefore applied to tents because of their being extended or spread out on the ground, so when it is applied to trees it must necessarily mean such as were remarkable for their widely-extended branches, but what the particular species is cannot be satisfactorily ascertained. By the Lord's planting are probably meant such trees as grow independently of the cultivation of man, Clarke says, as Virgil expresses it, such as sprung up spontaneously into the regions of light. On the cedars Clarke cites Gabriel Sionita, a very learned Syrian Maronite who assisted in editing the Paris Polyglot, a man worthy of all credit, who describes the cedars of Mount Lebanon which he had examined on the spot: the cedar grows on the most elevated part of the mountain, is taller than the pine, and so thick that five men together could scarcely fathom one; it shoots out its branches at ten or twelve feet from the ground, they are large and distant from each other and are perpetually green; the cedar distils a kind of gum to which different effects are attributed; the wood is of a brown colour, very solid, and incorruptible if preserved from wet; and it bears a small apple, like to that of the pine. Clarke also relates from de la Roque, who learned it from the Maronites of Mount Libanus, that the branches grow in parallel rows round the tree but lessen gradually from the bottom to the top, shooting out parallel to the horizon, so that the tree is in appearance similar to a cone; and that as the snows which fall in vast quantities on this mountain must necessarily by their weight break down these branches, nature, or rather the God of nature, has so ordered it that at the approach of winter and during the snowy season the branches erect themselves and cling close to the body of the tree, and thus prevent any quantity of snow from lodging on them. Clarke adds the report of Maundrell, who visited Mount Libanus in 1697: these noble trees grow among the snow near the highest part of Lebanon, and are remarkable as well for their own age and largeness as for those frequent allusions to them in the word of God; some of them are very old and of a prodigious bulk, others younger and of a smaller size, and of the former he could reckon only sixteen, but the latter are very numerous; he measured one of the largest and found it twelve yards and six inches in girth, and yet sound, and thirty-seven yards in the spread of its branches, and at about five or six yards from the ground it was divided into five limbs, each of which was equal to a great tree. On he shall pour the water out of his buckets, Clarke says here is a very plain allusion to their method of raising water in different parts of the East: by the well a tall pole is erected which serves as a fulcrum to a very long lever, to the smaller end of which a bucket is appended; on the opposite end, which is much larger, are many notches cut in the wood which serve as steps for a man whose business it is to climb up to the fulcrum in order to lower the bucket into the well, which when filled he raises by walking back on the opposite arm till his weight brings the bucket above the well's mouth, a person standing by the well emptying the bucket into a trench which communicates with the ground intended to be watered. His seed shall be in many waters is another simple allusion, to the sowing of rice, Clarke says: the ground must not only be well watered but flooded in order to serve for the proper growth of this grain, and the rice that was sown in many waters must be the most fruitful; by an elegant and chaste metaphor all this is applied to the procreation of a numerous posterity. On his king shall be higher than Agag, Clarke says this name is supposed to have been as common to all the Amalekitish kings as Pharaoh was to those of Egypt; but several critics, with the Septuagint, suppose that a small change has taken place here in the original word, and that instead of me-Agag, than Agag, we should read mig-Gog, than Gog, and as Gog in Scripture seems to mean the enemies of God's people, the promise here may imply that the true worshippers of the Most High shall ultimately have dominion over all their enemies. God brought him forth out of Egypt, Clarke says: they were neither expelled thence nor came voluntarily away, God alone with a high hand and uplifted arm brought them forth. These oracles delivered by Balaam are evident prophecies of the victories which the Israelites should gain over their enemies and of their firm possession of the promised land, Clarke concludes; they may also refer to the great victories to be obtained by the Lord Jesus Christ, that Lion of the tribe of Judah, over sin, death and Satan, the grand enemies of the human race, and to that most numerous posterity of spiritual children which should be begotten by the preaching of the Gospel. John Wesley says the vision is so called properly because he was awake when this was revealed to him, and that a trance means an ecstasy, fainting and falling upon the ground, as the prophets used to do. As the valleys means which often from a small beginning are spread forth far and wide, Wesley says; as gardens, pleasant and fruitful and secured by a fence; as lign aloes, an Arabian and Indian tree of a sweet smell, yielding shade and shelter both to man and beast, such is Israel, not only safe themselves but yielding shelter to all that join themselves to them; and which the Lord hath planted means nature, not art. He shall pour the water means that God will abundantly water the valleys, gardens and trees which represent the Israelites, Wesley says: he will wonderfully bless his people, not only with outward blessings, of which a chief one in those parts was plenty of water, but also with higher gifts and graces, with his word and spirit, which are often signified by water, and at last with eternal life, the contemplation whereof made Balaam desire to die the death of the righteous. His seed shall be in many waters may also be literally understood of their seed, which shall be sown in waterish ground and therefore bring forth a better increase, Wesley says. His King means the King of Israel, or their chief governor, and than Agag means than the King of the Amalekites, which King and people were famous and potent in that age, as may be guessed by their bold attempt upon so numerous a people as Israel, Wesley says; and it is probable that Agag was the common name of the Amalekitish Kings, as Abimelech was of the Philistines, and Pharaoh of the Egyptians, and Caesar of the Romans. He lay down means that, having conquered his enemies the Canaanites and their land, he shall quietly rest and settle himself there, Wesley concludes.

Charles Ellicott says that falling into a trance, but having his eyes open is better rendered falling upon his face and having his eyes opened, and that the physical effect produced upon Balaam appears to have been the same as that which was produced upon Saul, upon Ezekiel, upon Daniel and upon St. John. The word which is here rendered open, gelui, is a different word from that which is so rendered in the second verse, Ellicott says, and is frequently used in reference to divine communications and spiritual intuition; there may be a reference to the events which befell Balaam on his journey. On as gardens by the river's side, Ellicott says it is probable that the allusion may be to the Euphrates, although the definite article is not prefixed to the word nahar in the Hebrew. On as cedar trees beside the waters, the difference between cedars which grow beside running water which their roots can reach, and the ordinary type of cedars which throw out their strength in lateral branches, is illustrated in Ezekiel, where the proud Assyrian is compared to a cedar having his top among the thick boughs, or the clouds, which the waters made great, Ellicott says. He shall pour the water out of his buckets is better rendered water shall flow from his buckets, or he shall flow with water from his buckets, Ellicott says: the nation is personified as a man carrying two buckets full of water, which was the type and leading source of blessing and prosperity in the East, and this is a beautiful image, as Bishop Wordsworth has observed, of the true Israel pouring out the living waters of salvation, the pure streams of the Spirit, and making the wilderness of the world to rejoice and be glad. His seed shall be in many waters may mean that Israel should inhabit Canaan, a land of brooks of water, Ellicott says, or it may mean that, like seed sown and trees planted by the waters, they should inherit the richest blessings. Agag appears to have been the title, the nomen dignitatis, of the Amalekite kings, as Pharaoh of the Egyptian and Abimelech of the Philistine kings, Ellicott says; the reference does not seem to be to any particular king, but to the kingdom which should hereafter be established in Israel, to the kings generally which should come out of the loins of Abraham. On he couched, he lay down as a lion, and as a great lion, Ellicott says the Hebrew labi should be rendered a lioness, and that the image of a lion connects this verse with the preceding, he shall eat up the nations. On blessed is he that blesseth thee, Ellicott compares the original blessing which was pronounced upon Abraham by the Lord, and which was afterwards adopted by Isaac in the blessing which he pronounced upon Jacob. Keil and Delitzsch render the oracle, how beautiful are thy tents, O Jacob, thy dwellings, O Israel, like valleys are they spread out, like gardens by the stream, like aloes which Jehovah has planted, like cedars by the waters; water will flow out of his buckets, and his seed is by many waters; and loftier than Agag be his king, and his kingdom will be exalted. What Balaam had seen before his ecstasy with his bodily eyes formed the substratum for his inward vision, in which the dwellings of Israel came before his mental eye adorned with the richest blessing from the Lord, Keil says; the description starts, it is true, from the time then present, but it embraces the whole future of Israel. The word does not mean brooks here but valleys watered by brooks, Keil says, and the verb means to extend oneself, to spread out far and wide. Not only its dwellings, but Israel itself would also prosper abundantly, Keil says: it would have an abundance of water, that leading source of all blessing and prosperity in the burning East, and the nation is personified as a man carrying two pails overflowing with water, the dual form being generally used in connection with objects which are arranged in pairs. His seed means his posterity, not his sowing corn, the introduction of which in this connection would to say the least be very feeble here, Keil says, and it grows up by many waters, that is to say, enjoys the richest blessings; and the clause about the king is an optative, his king be high before, or higher than, Agag. Keil renders the remainder, God leads him out of Egypt, his strength is as that of a buffalo, he will devour nations his enemies and crush their bones and dash them in pieces with his arrows; he has encamped, he lies down like a lion, and like a lioness, who can drive him up; blessed be they who bless thee, and cursed they who curse thee. The fulness of power that dwelt in the people of Israel was apparent in the force and prowess with which their God brought them out of Egypt, Keil says, and Balaam repeats this fact from the previous saying for the purpose of linking on to it the still further announcement of the manner in which the power of the nation would show itself upon its foes in time to come; the words he will devour nations call up the image of a lion.

debates: Whether the text says Balaam fell into a trance: Clarke says flatly that it does not, the word being simply falling, perhaps a religious prostration, and the trance having been added by the translators; Ellicott renders the same word as falling upon his face but keeps the experience, comparing the physical effect on Saul, Ezekiel, Daniel and John; Keil translates falling down and with opened eyes; Wesley alone keeps both the vision and the ecstasy, glossing the trance as fainting and falling upon the ground, as the prophets used to do

Whether the sixth verse speaks of tents or of trees: Clarke notes that the word is identical with the tents of the previous verse and that the root fits both, then settles for a tree eight or ten feet high whose forests at a distance resemble an encampment, while admitting the species cannot be ascertained; Calvin decides for trees because the parallel clause names cedars; Wesley identifies it as an Arabian and Indian tree of sweet smell yielding shelter to man and beast, and reads Israel as sheltering all who join themselves to her

What his king shall be higher than Agag means: Ellicott and Wesley take Agag as a dynastic title like Pharaoh, Abimelech and Caesar, and refer the prophecy to the kingdom rather than to a man; Calvin agrees and explicitly rejects the conjecture that Saul and his captive Agag are meant, then extends the prophecy through David to Christ; Clarke reports critics who, with the Septuagint, read than Gog for than Agag on a small change in the original, which would make the promise dominion over all the enemies of God's people

How far the oracle reaches: Gill and Wesley keep it largely within Israel's history, the couching lion being the armies resting in a conquered Canaan; Calvin holds that Balaam, however little aware, embraced the time of David and predicted things only accomplished in Christ; Clarke likewise sees the victories of the Lion of the tribe of Judah over sin, death and Satan, and the spiritual posterity begotten by the Gospel
outliers: Clarke's three eyewitness reports of the cedars of Lebanon, from Gabriel Sionita, from de la Roque, and from Maundrell, who in 1697 measured one at twelve yards and six inches in girth and thirty-seven yards in the spread of its branches
The observation, reported by Clarke from the Maronites, that the cedar's branches erect themselves and cling to the trunk at the approach of winter so that snow cannot lodge on them and break them
Clarke's description of the well-lever, with its fulcrum pole, its notched arm and the man who climbs to lower the bucket and walks back to raise it
Clarke's second agricultural note, that the seed in many waters alludes to rice, whose ground must be flooded and not merely watered
Bishop Wordsworth's image, quoted by Ellicott, of the true Israel pouring out the living waters of salvation and making the wilderness of the world rejoice
Calvin's answer to the objection that Balaam blessed Israel and went unrewarded, namely that he deserved no reward, having been forcibly drawn where he was unwilling to go

10.pericope_label: Balak, enraged, smites his hands and dismisses Balaam without reward; Balaam pleads the constraint he had declared from the first and offers, before parting, to tell Balak what Israel will do to Moab in the latter days

schools.summary: John Gill says Balak's anger was kindled against Balaam, for he had borne much and long but could bear no longer, being quite impatient, and Balaam's last words more especially must exceedingly have nettled him. Therefore now flee thou to thy place means his own country, from whence Balak had sent for him and he came, Gill says: begone directly, make all haste away; he speaks as one so provoked that he could not bear him in his presence, and as threatening him if he did not at once get out of his sight. Balaam said unto Balak in order to mitigate his wrath and bring him into a better temper, Gill says, and his words about a house full of silver and gold are the very words he had said to the princes of Moab at the first. And now, behold, I go unto my people means, according to thine order, Gill says: I shall not stay to make thee uneasy with my company, only I crave thy patience to hear me a little before we part. John Calvin says that inasmuch as the obstinacy of the wicked is not overcome, so that they should submit themselves to God when he would bring their lusts under the yoke, it must needs be that when they are still further pressed they are carried away into passion; thus now Balak, after murmurings and expostulations, bursts forth into impetuous wrath, and rejects and drives away with reproaches from his presence Balaam, whom he had hitherto been endeavouring to cajole. When he smites his hands together it is because he can no longer restrain himself, Calvin says; he is especially indignant because Balaam had not hesitated freely and openly to bear witness to the blessing of the children of Israel, against whom he was so full of hatred, for nothing is more galling to kings than when they see private individuals regarding their presence at least without alarm. Since he determines to give no reward to the untoward and ill-starred prophet, he throws the blame upon God, lest he should himself incur discredit from this, as if he were illiberal, Calvin says; and indeed what he says is true, that God had kept back Balaam from honour, yet impiously, and as it were reproachfully, does he lay the blame upon God, and in fact accuses him of being the cause of the non-fulfilment of his promise. Balaam speaks the truth, indeed, yet in a bad spirit, Calvin says, for he excuses himself with servility to Balak, that it did not depend on himself that he did not comply with his wishes, but that God had stood in the way; for he grieves at the loss of his reward, and however grandly he may declaim on the supremacy of God, he still signifies that he has rather acted upon compulsion than willingly executed what was enjoined upon him. By the word of the Lord he means not only his decree but what had been dictated to him, and which he would have still greatly desired to alter, Calvin says, but he indicates that he was bound by the power of the Spirit to declare, even against his own will, whatever revelation he received. Thus the word do refers to his tongue, or his charge as a prophet, Calvin says, since he had not been hired by Balak to perform any manual act, but only to injure the people by his words; and the word heart is contrasted with the revelation of the Spirit, for impostors are said to speak out of their own heart when they falsely make use of God's name to cover their own inventions, so that he declares he was not at liberty to speak of his own heart, because he was the minister of the Spirit. Since the counsel which he gave is not here expressly mentioned, Calvin says, it is the opinion of some that his address is unfinished, and they suppose that he referred to the cunning advice so destructive to the people which will be presently related, that the Moabitish women should prostitute themselves; others rather imagine that Balaam counselled Balak to rest quiet, since the prosperity of the Israelites would do no harm to the Moabites in his lifetime. Calvin, however, takes it simply for to teach, or to admonish what would be for his advantage; thus he commends his prophecy, in order that Balak may willingly submit to it. Still, when he speaks of the latter days, he signifies that there was no cause for Balak himself to fear or be anxious, since the punishment of his nation would be deferred for a long time, Calvin says. In the meantime we see what Balak had gained by his trouble, Calvin concludes: for whereas he had hitherto only heard the people of Israel blessed, he is now compelled to listen to what is more painful still, namely the ruin of his own nation; and this is the reward of those who strive against God.

Matthew Henry says we have here the conclusion of this vain attempt to curse Israel and the total abandonment of it. Balak made the worst of it, breaking out into a rage against Balaam, expressed both in words and gesture, the highest degree of vexation at the disappointment, Henry says: he smote his hands together for indignation, to see all his measures thus broken and his project baffled. He charged Balaam with putting upon him the basest affront and cheat imaginable, Henry says, saying that he had called him to curse his enemies and Balaam had shown himself in league with them and in their interests, blessing them these three times, though by appointing the altars to be built and sacrifices to be offered he had made Balak believe he would certainly curse them. Hereupon he forbade him his presence, expelled him his country, and upbraided him with the preferments he had designed to bestow upon him but now would not, Henry says: the Lord hath kept thee back from honour, see what thou gettest by pleasing the Lord instead of pleasing me, thou hast hindered thy preferment by it. Thus those who are any way losers by their duty are commonly upbraided with it, as fools, for preferring it before their interest in the world, Henry says; whereas, if Balaam had been voluntary and sincere in his adherence to the word of the Lord, though he lost the honour Balak designed him by it, God would have made that loss up to him abundantly to his advantage. Balaam made the best of it, Henry says: he endeavours to excuse the disappointment, and a very good excuse he has for it, that God restrained him from saying what he would have said and constrained him to say what he would not, and that this was what Balak ought not to be displeased at, not only because he could not help it but because he had told Balak beforehand what he must depend upon; Balak could not say that he had cheated him, since he had given him fair notice of the check he found himself under. He endeavours to atone for it, Henry says: though he cannot do what Balak would have him do, he will gratify his curiosity with some predictions concerning the nations about him, for it is natural to us to be pleased with prophecy, and with this he hopes to pacify the angry prince. He will satisfy him with an assurance that, whatever this formidable people should do to his people, it should not be till the latter days, so that he for his part needed not fear any mischief or molestation from them, the vision being for a great while to come, but in his days there should be peace, Henry says. And he will put him into a method of doing Israel a mischief without the ceremonies of enchantment and execration, Henry says: this seems to be implied in that word, I will advertise thee, for it properly signifies, I will counsel thee; what the counsel was is not set down here, because it was given privately, but we are told afterwards, and he counselled him to entice the Israelites to idolatry. Since he could not have leave from God to curse them, he puts him in a way of getting help from the devil to tempt them, Henry concludes, quoting the line that if I cannot move the powers above, I will solicit hell.

Adam Clarke says that lo, the Lord hath kept thee back from honour is a bitter and impious sarcasm, as if Balak had said: hadst thou cursed this people, I would have promoted thee to great honour, but thou hast chosen to follow the directions of Jehovah rather than mine, and what will he do for thee? John Wesley reads the taunt the same way, glossing the Lord as meaning, whose commands thou hast preferred before my desires and interest, and therefore seek thy recompence from him, and not from me.

Charles Ellicott says that the smiting of the hands was a token of strong feeling, whether of scorn, of indignation, or of despair. On the words the Lord hath kept thee back from honour, Ellicott says these may have been spoken ironically, or Balak may have been convinced of the supernatural influence under which the words of Balaam were uttered. I cannot go beyond the commandment of the Lord is in Hebrew the mouth of the Lord, Ellicott notes, the same expression which is used earlier where the Authorised Version has the word of the Lord. On I go unto my people, Ellicott says such was probably the intention of Balaam when he spoke these words, though the account of the death of Balaam shows that he still lingered amongst the Moabites. The word rendered I will advertise thee generally means to advise, Ellicott says, and the announcement which Balaam made to Balak virtually included advice, inasmuch as it foretold the supremacy of Israel over all their foes and consequently implied the folly of opposition to their progress. It does not appear whether it was or was not at this time that Balaam taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols and to commit fornication, Ellicott says; in any case there does not appear to be any reference to such advice in this verse, although it is inserted in the Targum of Palestine in this place. In the latter days is literally in the end of the days, Ellicott says, and the prophecy which follows refers exclusively to the future, being divided into four parts by the recurrence of the words he took up his parable. Keil and Delitzsch say that Balaam reminds Balak, on the other hand, of the declaration which he made to the messengers at the very outset, that he could not on any account speak in opposition to the command of Jehovah. The verb rendered advertise means to advise, Keil says; here it denotes an announcement which includes advice, for the announcement of what Israel would do to the Moabites in the future contains advice to Balak on what attitude he should assume towards Israel, if this people was to bring a blessing upon his own people and not a curse. Keil notes that in the words the Lord hath kept thee back from honour, the irony with which Balak scoffs at Balaam's confidence in Jehovah is unmistakable, and that smiting the hands together is either a sign of horror or of violent rage, it being in the latter sense that it occurs here. Balaam's fourth and last prophecy is distinguished from the previous ones by the fact that it is occupied exclusively with the future, Keil says, and foretells the victorious supremacy of Israel over all its foes and the destruction of all the powers of the world; this prophecy is divided into four different prophecies by the fourfold repetition of the words, he took up his parable.

debates: Whether Balak's remark about honour is ironical: Clarke calls it a bitter and impious sarcasm and expands it into a speech; Wesley and Keil read it the same way, Keil calling the irony unmistakable; Ellicott alone allows the alternative, that Balak may by then have been convinced of the supernatural influence under which Balaam spoke; Calvin holds that the statement is true in itself but impiously made, since Balak lays on God the blame for a promise he himself is breaking

What Balaam means by offering to advertise Balak: Henry takes it as the private counsel to entice Israel into idolatry, so that failing to move heaven he solicits hell; Ellicott expressly denies that any such advice appears in this verse, noting that the Targum of Palestine inserts it here but that the word generally means only to advise, and that the announcement itself implied the folly of opposing Israel; Keil reads it benignly as advice on what attitude Balak should take so that Israel might bring his people a blessing; Calvin reports the sinister reading and a milder one, that Balaam advised Balak to rest quiet, and himself takes it simply as to teach or admonish

How far Balaam's excuse should be credited: Henry calls it a very good excuse and notes that Balak had fair notice of the check from the first; Keil and Ellicott simply record that he is repeating his opening declaration; Calvin grants that he speaks the truth but denies the spirit, saying he excuses himself with servility, grieves for his lost reward, and shows by his own words that he acted on compulsion and not willingly

What the latter days imply for Balak: Henry and Calvin agree that Balak is being assured the danger is distant, so that in his own days there should be peace; but Calvin adds that the assurance is no comfort, since Balak, having so far heard only Israel blessed, must now hear the ruin of his own nation
outliers: Calvin's observation that nothing is more galling to kings than to see private individuals regard their presence without alarm

Calvin's close reading of Balaam's three words, that the word of the Lord means the dictation and not merely the decree, that do refers to his tongue since he was hired only to injure by speech, and that of mine own heart is the mark of impostors who use God's name to cover their inventions
Ellicott's note that Balaam probably did intend to go home, though the account of his death shows that he still lingered among the Moabites
Henry's tag that one who cannot move the powers above will solicit hell
Ellicott's and Keil's shared observation that the fourth prophecy is divided into four by the fourfold repetition of he took up his parable
Calvin's closing sting, that what Balak gained by his trouble was to hear, after three blessings on Israel, the ruin of his own nation

15.pericope_label: Balaam takes up his fourth parable with the preface renewed, and sees, not now and not nigh, a Star coming out of Jacob and a Sceptre rising out of Israel to smite the corners of Moab

schools.summary: John Gill says the same preface in the same words is made to his prophecy as before, only one clause is added, and knew the knowledge of the Most High. That Balaam had some knowledge of God is certain from the names by which he calls him, being such that God made himself known by to the patriarchs and by which he is frequently called in the sacred writings, Gill says; but then this knowledge of his was merely notional and speculative, and not spiritual and supernatural, and was such as men may have who are destitute of the grace of God. He was one that professed to know him in words but in works denied him, Gill says, and he was also admitted to much nearness to God and converse with him, of which he boasted; but then this was not for his own sake, or as a mark of friendship to him, but for the sake of the people of Israel, and to prevent his doing them mischief. On I shall see him, but not now, Gill says he means not Israel, for he now saw him encamped and at no great distance, but one that should descend from him, a famous and excellent person, who is no other than the Messiah, as appears by what follows; him he should see, not spiritually with an eye of faith, nor corporeally with his bodily eyes in his state of incarnation, but at the day of judgment, and now indeed he saw him by a spirit of prophecy. John Calvin says that inasmuch as he was preparing to treat of most important matters, it is not without reason that he renews his preface, in order to obtain more authority for his prophecy; and although it was not without ambition that he proclaimed these magnificent titles, still we cannot doubt but that God would ratify by them what he had determined to deliver through the mouth of the prophet. It was requisite that this worthless man, whose doctrine would otherwise have been contemptible, should be marked out by divine indications, Calvin says, and thus it was that he assumed a character that he did not possess, and attributed to himself what only belongs to true prophets. Calvin has before explained how the open and the closed eye are spoken of in the same sense though for different reasons, for he calls the eye hidden as perceiving the secret things of darkness which are incomprehensible to the human sense, but he claims for himself open eyes in that he beholds by prophetic vision what he is about to say, as if he would deny that he was going to speak of things which were obscure and scarcely intelligible to himself. On I see him, Calvin says that though the verbs are in the future tense they are used for the present, and the pronoun designates some one who has not yet been mentioned, which is a tolerably common usage with the Hebrew, especially when referring to Jerusalem, or God, or some very distinguished man; and although there can be no doubt but that he alluded to the people of Israel, it is still a question whether he designates the head or the whole body, on which point Calvin does not make much contention, since it is substantially the same thing. The reason why Balaam postpones his prophecies to a distant period is in order to afford consolation to Balak, Calvin says, for as much as he possibly can he seeks to avoid his ill-will, and therefore assures him that although he denounces evil it was not to be feared at an early period. The second clause must unquestionably be restricted to the head of the people, called metaphorically a Star and then expressly referred to without a figure, Calvin says, for this repetition is common with the Hebrews; assuredly he means nothing else by the Sceptre except what he had indicated by the Star, and thus he connects the prosperity of the people with the kingdom. Hence we gather that its state was not perfect until it began to be governed by the hand of a king, Calvin says, for inasmuch as the adoption of the family of Abraham was founded on Christ, only sparks of God's blessing shone forth until its completed brightness was manifested in Christ; when Balaam begins to prophesy of God's grace towards the people of Israel he directs us at once to the sceptre, as if it were the true and certain mirror of God's favour, and in fact God never manifested himself as the Father of this people except by Christ. Calvin admits that some beginnings existed in the person of David, but they were very far from exhibiting the fullness of the reality, for the glory of his kingdom was not lasting, nay, its chief dignity was speedily impaired by the rebellion of the ten tribes and was finally altogether extinguished, and when David's power was at its height his dominion never extended beyond the neighbouring nations. The coming forth of the Star and the Sceptre therefore refers to Christ, Calvin says, and what we read in the Psalm corresponds with this prophecy, the Lord shall send the sceptre of thy strength out of Sion; hence it follows that the blessing of which Balaam speaks descends even to us, for if the prosperity of the ancient people, their rest, their well-ordered government, their dignity, safety and glory proceeded from the sceptre as its unmixed source, there is no doubt but that Christ by his coming accomplished all these things more fully for us. The destruction of the nation of Moab is added as an adjunct of the kingdom, Calvin says. Those who take the children of Sheth generally for the whole human race violently wrest the text by their gloss, Calvin says: Balaam is speaking of the neighbouring nations, and when in the next verse he goes on to specify Edom he adds Mount Seir by way of explanation; since the form of the two sentences is identical, it is probable that none others than the Moabites are meant by the children of Sheth. Still the question arises why Balaam attributes to a single nation what was common to all, Calvin says, for all who were of the descendants of Sheth equally derived their origin from Noah; some think that they boasted of this descent in order to conceal their shame, for we know that the founder of this nation sprang from an incestuous connection, but another more satisfactory reason occurs to Calvin, namely that they boasted, like the Amalekites, of the extreme antiquity of their race, so that since they desired to be reckoned amongst the most ancient nations it will not be improbable that by this ironical appellation their vain-glory was reproved. It may, however, have been the case that some one amongst the descendants of Moab was distinguished by this name, Calvin allows. The Moabites as well as the Edomites were subdued by David, for David thus justly celebrates his triumphs over them, Moab is my wash-pot, over Edom will I cast out my shoe, Calvin says; but then was merely typified what Christ at length fulfilled, in that he reduced under his sway all adverse and hostile nations.

Matthew Henry says the office of prophets was both to bless and to prophesy in the name of the Lord, and that Balaam as a prophet had perforce blessed Israel and here foretells future events. His preface is much the same as the earlier one, Henry says: he personates a true prophet admirably well, God permitting and directing him to do so because, whatever he was, the prophecy itself was a true prophecy. He boasts that his eyes are open, for prophets were in old time called seers because they must speak what they had seen, and therefore before they opened their lips it was necessary that they should have their eyes open, Henry says. He boasts that he has heard the words of God, which many do that do not heed them, nor hear God in them; and that he knew the knowledge of the Most High, which is added here, for a man may be full of the knowledge of God and yet utterly destitute of the grace of God, may receive the truth in the light of it and yet be a stranger to the love of it, Henry says. And he boasts that he saw the vision of the Almighty, but not so as to be changed into the same image, Henry says: he calls God the Most High and the Almighty, and no man could speak more honourably of him nor seem to put a greater value upon his acquaintance with him, and yet he had no true fear of him, love to him, or faith in him, so far may a man go towards heaven and yet come short. Here is his prophecy concerning him that should be the crown and glory of his people Israel, Henry says, who is David in the type, who not now, not quickly, but in process of time should smite the corners of Moab and take possession of Mount Seir, which was fulfilled when David smote Moab and measured them with a line, so that the Moabites became David's servants. But our Lord Jesus, the promised Messiah, is chiefly pointed at in the antitype, Henry says, and of him it is an illustrious prophecy; it was the will of God that notice should thus be given of his coming a great while before, not only to the people of the Jews but to other nations, because his gospel and kingdom were to extend themselves so far beyond the borders of the land of Israel. Balaam, a wicked man, shall see Christ, but shall not see him nigh, nor see him as Job, who saw him as his Redeemer and saw him for himself, Henry says: when he comes in the clouds every eye shall see him, but many will see him, as the rich man in hell saw Abraham, afar off. He shall come out of Jacob and Israel as a star and a sceptre, the former denoting his glory and lustre and the bright and morning star, the latter his power and authority, Henry says. Perhaps this prophecy of Balaam, one of the children of the east, concerning a star that should arise out of Jacob as the indication of a sceptre arising in Israel, being preserved by a tradition of that country, gave occasion to the wise men, who were of the east too, upon the sight of an unusual star over the land of Judea, to enquire for him that was born king of the Jews, Henry says. His kingdom shall be universal and victorious over all opposition, which was typified by David's victories over Moab and Edom, Henry says: the Messiah shall destroy, or as some read it shall rule over, all the children of Seth, that is, all the children of men who descend from Seth the son of Adam, the descendants of the rest of Adam's sons being cut off by the deluge. Christ shall be king not only of Jacob and Israel but of all the world, Henry says, so that all the children of Seth shall be either governed by his golden sceptre or dashed in pieces by his iron rod; he shall set up a universal rule, authority and power of his own, and shall put down all opposing rule. He shall unwall all the children of Seth, so some read it, Henry says: he shall take down all their defences and carnal confidences, so that they shall either admit his government or lie open to his judgments.

Adam Clarke says it seems strange that our version should have fallen into such a mistake as to render shethum open, which it does not signify, when the very sound of the word expresses the sense; the Vulgate has very properly preserved the true meaning by rendering the clause he whose eyes are shut, while the Targum first paraphrased the passage falsely, and most of the versions followed it. On I shall see him, but not now, Clarke renders it, I shall see him, but he is not now; and on I shall behold him, but not nigh, I shall have a full view of him, but the time is yet distant, that is, the person of whom I am now prophesying does not at present exist among these Israelites, nor shall he appear in this generation. There shall come a Star out of Jacob and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel means that a person eminent for wisdom and formidable for strength and power shall arise as king among this people, Clarke says; he shall smite the corners of Moab, that is, he shall bring the Moabites perfectly under subjection. The original word karkar is variously translated, Clarke reports: he shall waste, in the Vulgate; shall prey on, in the Septuagint; shall rule over, in the Targum; shall shake, in the Arabic; shall put a yoke on, in the Persian; shall unwall, in Ainsworth. The Targum of Onkelos translates the whole passage thus, Clarke says: I shall see him, but not now, I shall behold him, but he is not near; when a king shall arise from the house of Jacob, and the Messiah be anointed from the house of Israel, he shall slay the princes of Moab and rule over all the children of men. The Jerusalem Targum is a little different, Clarke says: a king shall arise from the house of Jacob, a redeemer and governor from the house of Israel, who shall slay the chiefs of the Moabites and empty out and destroy all the children of the East. Rabbi Moses ben Maimon has, in Clarke's opinion, perfectly hit the meaning of the prophecy in his paraphrase of the text: I shall see him, but not now, this is David; I shall behold him, but not nigh, this is the king Messiah; a Star shall come out of Jacob, this is David; and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, this is the king Messiah; and shall smite the corners of Moab, this is David, as it is written, and he smote Moab, casting them down to the ground; and shall destroy all the children of Sheth, this is the king Messiah, of whom it is written, he shall have dominion from sea to sea. John Wesley says I shall see him means, I have seen, or do see, the star and sceptre as it here follows, that is, a great and eminent prince which was to come out of Israel's loins, the Messiah, as both Jewish and Christian interpreters expound it, who most eminently and fully performed what is here said in destroying the enemies of Israel or of God's church, here described under the names of the nearest and fiercest enemies of Israel. To him alone agrees the foregoing verb properly, I shall see him, in my own person, as every eye shall see him when he comes to judgment, Wesley says; and not now means not yet, but after many ages. A star is a title often given to princes and eminent persons, and particularly to the Messiah, Wesley says, and a sceptre means a sceptre-bearer, a king or ruler, even that sceptre mentioned in Genesis. The corners means the borders, which are often used in scripture for the whole country to which they belong, Wesley says. Of Sheth seems to be the name of some then eminent, though now unknown, place or prince in Moab, Wesley concludes, there being innumerable instances of such places or persons sometime famous but now utterly lost as to all monuments and remembrances of them.

Charles Ellicott says that which heard and knew is better rendered which heareth and knoweth, and which saw is better he seeth. On I shall see him, Ellicott renders it, I see him, or it, but not now; I behold him, but not nigh; the reference cannot be to Israel, whose armies were encamped before the eyes of Balaam, and his words must be understood as having reference to One whom he beheld with the eyes of his mind, not with his bodily sight, which is obvious from the words which follow. Balaam beholds in vision a Star and a Sceptre, not as having already appeared but as about to appear in the future, Ellicott says. There shall come a Star out of Jacob is literally there hath come forth a Star out of Jacob, the verb being in the prophetic past or historic tense of prophecy, denoting the certainty of the event predicted, Ellicott says, comparing the Epistle of Jude where behold the Lord cometh is literally came. If there is any ambiguity in the first symbol it is removed in the second, Ellicott says: a star is a fitting image of an illustrious king or ruler, and the mention of the sceptre in the words which follow shows that it is so employed in the present instance. The Targum of Onkelos reads, when the King shall arise out of Jacob, and the Messiah shall be anointed from Israel, Ellicott reports, and the Targum of Palestine reads, a King is to arise from the house of Jacob, and a Redeemer and Ruler from the house of Israel; Ibn Ezra interprets these words of David, but he says that many interpret them of the Messiah. It seems to have been with reference to this prophecy that the pretender to the title of the Messiah in the days of the Emperor Adrian took the name of Bar-cochab, the son of a star, Ellicott says, and the words of the Magi, we have seen his star in the East, appear to have reference to this prophecy. And shall smite the corners of Moab means the two sides of Moab, Ellicott says, and the prophecy was partially, or typically, fulfilled in the time of David; Moab and Edom represented symbolically the enemies of Christ and of his Church, and as such will eventually be subdued by the King of kings. And destroy all the children of Sheth is better rendered and destroy, or break down, all the sons of tumult, Ellicott says, such appearing to be the most probable rendering of these words according to the present Hebrew text; it has been conjectured, however, that the word which is rendered destroy should be read as crown of the head, as in the parallel passage of Jeremiah, in which case the clause may be rendered, and the crown of the head of all the sons of tumult. Keil and Delitzsch say the prophecy itself commences with a picture from the end of the days which rises up before the mental eye of the seer: I see him, yet not now; I behold him, but not nigh; a star appears out of Jacob, and a sceptre rises out of Israel, and dashes Moab in pieces on both sides, and destroys all the sons of confusion. The suffixes refer to the star which is mentioned afterwards, and which Balaam sees in spirit, but not now, that is, not as having already appeared, and not nigh, that is, not to appear immediately, but to come forth out of Israel in the far distant future, Keil says.

debates: Who the children of Sheth are: Henry takes them universally, as all mankind descended from Seth the son of Adam, the other lines having perished in the deluge, so that all must either accept Christ's sceptre or be broken by it; Calvin says that reading violently wrests the text, since the parallel clause names Edom and Mount Seir, and holds that only the Moabites are meant, the title being either their boast of ancient descent ironically reproved or a cover for the incest their nation sprang from; Wesley guesses at some then eminent but now wholly forgotten place or prince in Moab; Ellicott and Keil abandon the proper name altogether and render sons of tumult or of confusion

Whether the Star is David or the Messiah: Clarke reports Maimonides dividing the verse clause by clause between the two and calls it a perfect hit at the meaning; Henry gives the same as type and antitype; Ellicott reports both Targums and Ibn Ezra, who reads David while noting that many read Messiah, and adds that the prophecy was partially or typically fulfilled under David; Calvin agrees that David is in it but denies he is enough, since the glory of his kingdom was neither lasting nor extensive and was finally extinguished

How the word rendered destroy should be taken: Clarke lists six renderings from six versions, he shall waste, shall prey on, shall rule over, shall shake, shall put a yoke on, and shall unwall; Ellicott takes it as break down but reports a conjecture that it should be repointed to give the crown of the head, as in the parallel in Jeremiah; Keil renders it destroys

Whether Balaam's word open can stand: Clarke returns to the crux a second time at this verse, calling it strange that our version renders the word open when it does not signify that, praising the Vulgate for the true sense and blaming the Targum for a false paraphrase that most versions followed; Calvin instead reconciles the two senses, the eye being hidden as perceiving what is incomprehensible to human sense and open as beholding by prophetic vision what he is about to speak
outliers: Henry's warning that a man may be full of the knowledge of God and yet utterly destitute of the grace of God, receiving the truth in the light of it while remaining a stranger to the love of it
Henry's conjecture that Balaam, one of the children of the east, left a tradition in that country which led the wise men of the east to look for a star over Judea
Ellicott's note that the pretender under the Emperor Adrian took the name Bar-cochab, son of a star, from this prophecy
Ellicott's observation that the verb is the prophetic past, there hath come forth, denoting the certainty of the event, as when Jude writes that the Lord came
Henry's image that the children of Seth shall be either governed by Christ's golden sceptre or dashed in pieces by his iron rod
Calvin's remark that Balaam postpones his prophecies to a distant period partly to console Balak and avoid his ill-will

18.pericope_label: The oracle turns to the neighbouring nations: Edom and Seir become a possession, a ruler comes out of Jacob to destroy the remnant of the cities, Amalek the first of the nations perishes for ever, and the Kenite is secure in his rocky nest

schools.summary: John Gill says Edom shall be a possession of the children of Israel, which was fulfilled in part when the Edomites became the servants of David, and when they were smitten and spoiled by Judas Maccabeus, and still more so when all the Edomites or Idumaeans were subdued by Hyrcanus and they became one people with the Jews and conformed to their religious rites; which is not only related by Josephus but by Strabo, an heathen historian, who says that they joined themselves to the Jews and embraced their laws. But in a spiritual sense this has had a greater accomplishment in the calling of the Gentiles and introducing them into the church of God, Gill says. Out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion means either David, or rather the Messiah, Gill says, and so Jarchi interprets this of another ruler out of Jacob, even of the Messiah, of whom it is said, he shall have dominion from sea to sea. When he looked on Amalek means the country of Amalek, which lay to the south of the land of Canaan, and which Balaam had a view of from the mountain of Peor where he now was, Gill says. And he looked on the Kenites: not the family and posterity of Jethro, as Aben Ezra, Jarchi and Abendana suppose, Gill says, for they were not a people by themselves but were now encamped with Israel and went with them into the land of Canaan, and were not carried captive with the ten tribes, though some might that dwelt in Naphtali, for they after that remained with Judah under the name of Rechabites and returned with the two tribes, being carried captive with them; but they were a people, though of the same original and family that Jethro descended from, which dwelt near and afterwards among the Amalekites, and therefore were seen by Balaam and taken notice of at the same time they were. John Calvin says this people had already been destined to destruction by a divine decree, but what God had before declared is here again ratified by Moses; although the vengeance which God was about to take lay dormant for many ages, it was at length experimentally proved that God had not threatened in vain. But whilst it is true that they were destroyed by Saul, still we learn from the history that some still survived and again inhabited their land, Calvin says; in order therefore to arrive at the entire accomplishment of this prophecy we must come to Christ, whose kingdom is the eternal destruction of all the wicked. Poor and unsatisfactory is the view of some commentators who think that Amalek is called the first of the nations because they first took up arms against Israel and encountered them in order to prevent their advance, Calvin says: rather is the pride of Amalek indirectly rebuked, because they claimed superiority for themselves over other nations, and this on the score of their antiquity, as if they had been created together with the sun and moon; there is then a pointed comparison between this noble origin and the slaughter which awaited them at their end. Calvin has not yet referred to the sense in which Balaam is said to have seen the Kenites as well as the other nations, and would now also refrain from doing so, if some did not attribute it to prophetical vision, in which opinion he cannot agree; for Moses relates as a matter of history that Balaam turned his face in the directions in which they respectively lived, and although he did not actually see the people themselves, the sight of the place in which they dwelt was sufficient for the purpose of prophecy. By the Kenites Calvin understands the Midianites, who were contiguous to the Amalekites, for it is altogether unreasonable to refer the name to the descendants of Jethro: forty years had not yet elapsed since Jethro had left his son with Moses, and his was only one small family in the wilderness of Midian, whereas mention is here made of a people already celebrated. Balaam therefore designates the Midianites and devotes them also to the punishment they well deserved, Calvin says; of this Gideon was in some measure the minister and executioner, when he routed their immense army with three hundred men, and his victory is celebrated in the Psalm and in Isaiah, so that it is probable their power was broken at that time.

Adam Clarke says that Edom shall be a possession, that is, to David, as it is said, and all they of Edom became David's servants; and Seir also shall be a possession, that is, unto the king Messiah, as it is said, and saviours shall come upon Mount Zion to judge the Mount of Esau, and the kingdom shall be the Lord's. On out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion, Clarke says this is supposed to refer to Christ, and that it is exceedingly difficult to fix the true sense of this prophecy in all its particulars; probably the star is only an emblem of kingly power, and among the Egyptians a star is said to have been the symbol of the Divine Being, while the sceptre refers to the kingly power in exercise, and the corners or outskirts may mean the petty Moabitish governments, as the Chaldee has understood the term.
