As neither Israel nor the Messiah ever destroyed all the children of men, Clarke says, we must, in order to leave the children of Sheth what they are generally understood to be, all the inhabitants of the world, understand the whole as a prophecy of the final universal sway of the sceptre of Christ, when the middle wall of partition shall be broken down and the Jews and Gentiles become one united, blended fold under one shepherd and bishop of their souls. Clarke cannot think that the meteoric star which guided the wise men of the east to Bethlehem can be intended here, nor does he think that Peter refers to this prophecy when he calls Christ the day star, nor that the places where Christ is called the morning star and the bright and morning star refer at all to this prophecy of Balaam. Nor does Clarke think that the false Christ who rose in the time of Adrian, and who called himself Barcochab, which literally signifies the son of a star, did refer to this prophecy: if he had, he must have defeated his own intention, because the Son of the star is not The Star that should arise, but at the utmost a descendant, and then, to vindicate his right to the Jewish throne, he must show that the person who was called the star, and of whom he pretended to be the son or descendant, had actually reigned before him. As the sun, moon, stars, planets, light, splendours, day and the like were always considered among the Asiatics as emblems of royalty and government, therefore many, both men and women, had these names given to them as titles and surnames, Clarke says: so the queen of Alexander the Great, called Roxana by the Greeks, was a Persian princess, and in her native tongue her name was Roushen, splendour; and Hadassah, who became queen to Ahasuerus, is called in the language of Persia Sitareh, from whence by corruption came both Esther, the Persian queen, and our word star. Clarke adds the case of a Mohammedan prince, at first named Joseph, who was called Roushen Akhter when he was raised to the throne, which signifies a splendid or luminous star, being brought from a gloomy prison and exalted to the throne of Hindostan, on which account a couplet was made playing on his name: he was a bright star, but is now become a moon; Joseph is brought out of prison, and is become a glorious king. On Amalek was the first of the nations, Clarke says this means the most ancient and most powerful of all the nations or states then within the view of Balaam, but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever, or his posterity shall be destroyed or shall utterly fail. This oracle began to be fulfilled by Saul, who overthrew the Amalekites and took their king Agag prisoner, Clarke says; afterwards they were nearly destroyed by David, and they were finally exterminated by the sons of Simeon in the days of Hezekiah, since which time they have ceased to exist as a people, and now no vestige of them remains on the face of the earth, so completely is their posterity cut off according to this prophecy. On the Kenites, Clarke says commentators are not well agreed who they were, and that Dr. Dodd's opinion is nearest to the truth: Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, is called a priest or prince of Midian and elsewhere a Kenite, so we may infer that the Kenites and the Midianites were the same, or at least confederate tribes; some of these followed the Israelites, others abode still among the Midianites and Amalekites, and when Saul destroyed the latter we find he had no commission against the Kenites, for it appears that they were then a small and inconsiderable people, having doubtless been wasted, as the text says, though by what means does not appear from history. On the other hand, Clarke observes, the Midianites mentioned here lived close to the Dead Sea, at a great distance from the Midian where Jethro lived, which was near Horeb, so that perhaps they were a colony or tribe that had migrated from the vicinity of Mount Sinai. It seems that at this time the Kenites occupied a very strong position, Clarke says, and there is a play on the original word, which signifies both a Kenite and a nest; high rocks in these countries were generally used as their strong places. John Wesley says a possession was also foretold to Rebekah and in part fulfilled under David, but more fully by Christ, who shall subdue and possess all his enemies, here signified by the name of Edom, as Jacob or Israel his brother signifies all his church and people; and Seir is a part and mountain of Edom. Out of Jacob means out of Jacob's loins, Wesley says, and he that shall have dominion means David, and especially Christ; of the city means from or out of the cities, the singular number for the plural, for he shall not subdue only those Moabites and Edomites which meet him in the field, but he shall pursue them even to their strongest holds and cities. He looked on Amalek from the top of Pisgah, which was exceeding high and gave him the prospect of part of all these kingdoms, Wesley says; and the first is in Hebrew the firstfruits, so called either because they were the first of all the neighbouring nations which were embodied together in one government, or because he was the first who fought against Israel and was vanquished by them, that victory being an earnest and firstfruit of the large harvest of victories which the Israelites should in due time get over all their enemies. He shall perish for ever, Wesley says: he began with God and with Israel, but God will end with him, and the firm purpose of God is that he shall be utterly destroyed, so that Saul lost his kingdom for not executing this decree. The Kenites are the posterity or kindred of Jethro, Wesley says, not that part of them which dwelt among the Israelites, to whom the following words do not agree, but those of them who were mingled with the Amalekites and Midianites; and thy nest means thy dwelling-place, so called either because it was in a high place, as nests commonly are, or in allusion to their name, for the Hebrew word signifies a nest.

Charles Ellicott says the verse is better rendered, and Edom shall be a possession, and Seir shall be a possession, for his enemies, that is, the enemies of Israel, or rather of the Ruler who was to rise out of Israel; the Hebrew word rendered his enemies appears to stand in apposition to Edom and Seir, just as the corresponding word earlier in the chapter stands in apposition to the nations. Edom was the name of the people, Seir of the country, Ellicott says; the prophecy received its primary accomplishment in the time of David, but the ultimate accomplishment is to be found in the person and work of Christ, and Israel shall do valiantly may also be rendered shall acquire power or wealth. On he that shall have dominion, Ellicott says the reference is explained in the Psalm, he shall have dominion also from sea to sea and from the river unto the ends of the earth, where the same verb occurs. And shall destroy him that remaineth of the city is better rendered, and he shall destroy the remnant from the cities, Ellicott says: the city, which is in the singular number here as in the Psalm, may be used collectively to denote cities generally, though some have understood the reference to be to the city of Jerusalem, but the reference seems rather to be to the chief city, or the cities generally, of Edom. From the mountain of Peor on which Balaam then stood he had a view of the country of the Amalekites, which lay to the south of the land of Canaan, Ellicott says. The ancestor of the Amalekites was Eliphaz, the son of Esau, and it has been supposed that the Amalekites separated themselves at a very early period from the rest of the Edomites, Ellicott says. The word which is here rendered first may denote priority in rank, but more frequently denotes priority in time, Ellicott says, and the corresponding word in the second clause, latter end, may be thought to denote that the reference is to time and not to rank; on the other hand, the earlier reference to the kings of the Amalekites may be urged in favour of the reference to rank, while some understand the allusion to be to the fact that the Amalekites were the first nation which attacked Israel when they had come out of Egypt; it is possible, however, that there may be a reference both to time and to rank. But his latter end shall be that he perish for ever is more literally, his latter end shall be even to one perishing, that is, he shall come to the position of one who is perishing, Ellicott says; the destruction of the Amalekites began in the reign of Saul, was continued by David, and was completed by Hezekiah. Keil and Delitzsch render the verse, and Edom becomes a possession, and Seir becomes a possession, its enemies, but Israel acquires power; whose possession Edom and Seir are to become is not expressly stated, but it is evident from the context and from the phrase its enemies, which is not a genitive dependent upon Seir but is in apposition to Edom and Seir. Edom and Seir were Israel's enemies, therefore they were to be taken by the ruler who was to arise out of Israel, Keil says; Edom is the name of the people, Seir of the country, so that Seir is not to be understood as relating to the pre-Edomitish population of the land. On the ruler, Keil says the subject is indefinite and to be supplied from the verb itself, and we have to think of the ruler foretold as star and sceptre; the word for city is employed in a collective and general sense, so that out of every city in which there is a remnant of Edom it shall be destroyed, and the explanation that the remnant is destroyed out of the holy city of Jerusalem is forced, and cannot be sustained from the parallelism. Balaam sees the Amalekites, not with the eyes of his body but in a state of ecstasy, like the star out of Jacob, Keil says, and the saying runs, beginning of the heathen is Amalek, and its end is destruction. Amalek is called the beginning of the nations not as belonging to the most distinguished and foremost of the nations in age, power and celebrity, as Knobel supposes, Keil says, for in all these respects this Bedouin tribe, which descended from a grandson of Esau, was surpassed by many other nations, but as the first heathen nation which opened the conflict of the heathen nations against Israel as the people of God; as its beginning had been enmity against Israel, its end would be even to the perishing, which commenced under Saul and was completed under Hezekiah. The third saying relates to the Kenites, whose origin is involved in obscurity, Keil says, as there are no other Kenites mentioned in the whole of the Old Testament than the Kenites who went to Canaan with Hobab the brother-in-law of Moses; so that there are not sufficient grounds for the distinction between Canaanitish and Midianitish Kenites, as Michaelis, Hengstenberg and others suppose, and the hypothesis that Balaam is speaking of Canaanitish Kenites, or of the Kenites as representatives of the Canaanites, is as unfounded as the hypothesis that by the Kenites we are to understand the Midianites.

debates: Who the Kenites are: Wesley makes them the kindred of Jethro, but only the part mingled with the Amalekites and Midianites; Gill refuses Jethro's family outright, against Aben Ezra and Jarchi, since those were encamped with Israel and went into Canaan, and allows only a people of the same stock settled near Amalek; Clarke follows Dodd in identifying Kenites and Midianites as the same or confederate tribes, while noting that the Midianites here lived far from Jethro's Midian near Horeb; Calvin says flatly that by the Kenites he understands the Midianites and calls it altogether unreasonable to refer the name to Jethro's descendants; Keil argues from Old Testament usage that no Kenites are known but those who came with Hobab, and calls the identification with Midian unfounded

Why Amalek is called the first of the nations: Clarke takes it as the most ancient and most powerful state then in Balaam's view; Keil expressly denies that, naming Knobel, since a Bedouin tribe from a grandson of Esau was surpassed by many nations in age and power, and refers it to Amalek's being the first heathen nation to open the conflict against Israel; Calvin as expressly rejects the first-to-attack reading as poor and unsatisfactory and finds an ironical rebuke of Amalekite pride in antiquity; Ellicott weighs the philology both ways and allows that both time and rank may be meant; Wesley reports both without deciding

What the remnant of the city means: Ellicott renders the remnant from the cities, taking the singular collectively of the cities of Edom rather than of Jerusalem; Keil agrees and calls the Jerusalem reading forced and unsustainable by the parallelism; Wesley reaches the same sense practically, that the ruler pursues his enemies to their strongest holds and does not merely beat them in the field

Whether the Star has anything to do with the star of Bethlehem or with Bar-cochba: Clarke denies both, and denies that Peter's day star or the morning star of the Revelation refer to this prophecy, arguing that a son of a star is not the Star, so the pretender would first have had to show that his claimed ancestor had reigned; this stands directly against the readings collected on the preceding verses
outliers: Gill's report that the submission of the Idumaeans under Hyrcanus, and their conforming to Jewish rites, is attested not only by Josephus but by the heathen historian Strabo
Clarke's excursus on stars as titles of royalty among the Asiatics, with Roxana whose Persian name meant splendour, and Esther whose Persian name is the ancestor of our word star
The Persian couplet Clarke quotes on the prince Roushen Akhter, that he was a bright star but is now become a moon, Joseph being brought out of prison and made a glorious king
Clarke's note that the Kenites had by Saul's day been wasted, though by what means does not appear from history
Calvin's insistence that Balaam's seeing of the Kenites was not prophetic vision but literal sight of the country they lived in, which was sufficient for the purpose of prophecy
Wesley's observation that the defeat of Amalek was an earnest and firstfruit of the harvest of victories Israel would afterwards gain
Calvin's assignment of the breaking of Midianite power to Gideon, who routed their immense army with three hundred men

22.pericope_label: The last sayings: the Kenite wasted until Asshur leads him captive, the cry of who shall live when God does this, ships from Chittim afflicting Asshur and Eber, and the parting of Balaam and Balak

schools.summary: John Gill says that though the Kenites were so strongly fortified, and closely immured and surrounded with rocks and mountains, yet they should gradually waste away, as they were but few in Saul's time. On the following verse Gill says only that Balaam delivered another prophecy, having made some little pause. Kittim was the son of Javan, and so designs some part of Greece, Gill says: Josephus says that Kittim possessed the island now called Cyprus, in which was a city called Citium after his name, while Macedonia, a considerable part of Greece, is called the land of Cittim in the book of Maccabees, where Alexander son of Philip the Macedonian is said to have come out of the land of Chettiim, and where Philip and Perseus are called kings of the Citims. But the Targum of Jonathan interprets it of the country of Italy, and the Jerusalem Targum of the Roman legions, Gill says, and perhaps both Greeks and Romans are intended, and so ships from Cittim design Romans in Grecian ships, for in such were the Roman ambassadors carried who distressed Antiochus king of Syria; and both may be intended here. Balaam rose up and went and returned to his place, that is, the country from whence he came, Gill says: he went from Balak according to his command in order to return to his own land, for he seems not to have reached it, but stayed by the way among the Moabites and Midianites and was slain in a battle between Israel and them; or if he did reach Mesopotamia he returned again, as Chaskuni says. Either before he left Balak, or in his journey homewards, or when he returned, he gave that advice to seduce the Israelites first to whoredom and by that to idolatry, the effects of which are observed in the following chapter, Gill says; and Balak also went his way to his royal city, court and family, attended very probably by the princes of Moab who had been with him all this while, though how long these things were transacting is not certain. John Calvin says it is a harsh and unnatural construction to apply this to the Kenites, and the majority indeed consent that it should be referred to the Israelites, yet they differ as to the meaning of it, for some take it affirmatively, that the Kenites should be wasted until the Assyrians should conquer the Israelites and carry them away captive, while some take it interrogatively, as if it were an abrupt exclamation, how long shall Asshur hold thee captive, thus conceiving that the prolonged exile of the people is indicated. Undoubtedly it was the purpose of the Spirit to show, by way of correction, that their prosperity which had been previously mentioned should be mixed with heavy afflictions, Calvin says, for slavery is a bitter thing and exile even worse; hence we gather that, though the Church is blessed by God, it is still in such a way as that it shall not cease to be exposed to various calamities, and the interrogation therefore will be most appropriate. It is unquestionable that the word Chittim is sometimes used for the Greeks, Calvin says: some indeed imagine that the Macedonians alone are strictly called by this name, but it is plain that it is applied generally to the whole of Greece; and since the countries beyond the sea were not so well known to the Jews as to allow of their distinguishing them, Scripture sometimes transfers this same name to Italy. Without doubt in Daniel the ships of Chittim must be taken for those of Italy or Rome, Calvin says, because the angel there predicts that the ships of Chittim would come which should overcome and render frustrate the efforts of Antiochus, which was plainly brought to pass by the mission of Popilius. With regard to the present passage, first of all the Greeks under Alexander afflicted both Judea and Assyria, and then another affliction followed at the hands of the Romans, Calvin says; since, however, Balaam has begun to prophesy of the kingdom of Christ, it is probable that the Romans are included together with the Greeks. From hence we more clearly perceive that the children of God are not so exempted from common evils as not to be often involved in them promiscuously with unbelievers, as if their conditions were precisely identical, Calvin says; although the Hebrews are placed on a par with the Assyrians as their companions in misfortune, still a consolation is added, that the Assyrians also shall perish like Chittim, when they have persecuted the Church. What Moses adds in conclusion, namely that Balaam returned to his people and Balak also went to his place, tends to the commendation of God's grace, since he dissipates the evil counsels of the wicked like clouds and overthrows their machinations, Calvin says; the sum is that the enemies of the chosen people departed in dishonour without accomplishing their purpose, since God put them to confusion.

Adam Clarke says the Assyrians and Babylonians who carried away captive the ten tribes, and the Jews into Babylon, probably carried away the Kenites also; indeed this seems pretty evident, as we find some Kenites mentioned among the Jews after their return from the Babylonish captivity. On who shall live when God doeth this, Clarke says there are two senses in which these words may be taken: that the event is so distant that none then alive could possibly live to see it, or that the times would be so distressing and desolating that scarcely any should be able to escape; the words are very similar to those of our Lord, and probably are to be taken in the same sense, woe to them that are with child, and to them that give suck in those days. On ships from the coast of Chittim, Clarke says some think the Romans and others the Macedonians under Alexander are meant; it is certain that the Romans did conquer the Assyrians, including all the people of Syria and Mesopotamia, but Calmet strongly contends that by Chittim Macedonia is meant and that the prophecy refers to the conquests of Alexander. Chittim was one of the sons of Javan, the son of Japheth, the son of Noah, Clarke says, and his posterity, according to Josephus, settled in Cilicia, Macedonia, Cyprus and Italy also, and therefore, says Ainsworth, the prophecy may imply both the troubles that befell the Assyrians and Jews by the Greeks and Seleucidae in the troublous days of Antiochus. And shall afflict Eber means probably not the Hebrews, as some think, but the people on the other side the Euphrates, from the verb to pass over or go beyond, all which people were discomfited and their empire destroyed by Alexander the Great, Clarke says. Balaam intended to have gone to Mesopotamia, his native country, but seems to have settled among the Midianites, where he was slain by the Israelites, Clarke says; and he then offers a series of propositions. It appears sufficiently evident that Balaam knew and worshipped the true God; that he had been a true prophet, and appears to have been in the habit of receiving oracles from God; that he practised some illicit branches of knowledge, or was reputed by the Moabites as a sorcerer, probably because of the high reputation he had for wisdom, as even in our own country persons who excelled their contemporaries in wisdom were reputed magicians; that though he was a believer in the true God yet he was covetous, and loved the wages of unrighteousness; that it does not appear that in the case before us he wished to curse Israel when he found they were the servants of the true God; and that it is possible he did not know this at first, since Balak told him only that a numerous people had come out of Egypt, and as wandering hordes and freebooters were frequent in those days he might take them at first for such spoilers. Clarke continues that so conscientiously did he act in the whole business that as soon as he found it displeased God he cheerfully offered to return, and did not advance till he had not only the permission but the authority of God to proceed; that when he came in view of the Israelitish camp he did not attempt to make use of any means of sorcery, evocation of spirits or necromantic spells to accomplish the wish of Balak; that he did seek to find out the will of the true God by using those means which God himself had prescribed, namely supplication and prayer and the sacrifice of the clean beasts; that though he knew it would greatly displease Balak, yet he most faithfully and firmly told him all that God said on every occasion; and that notwithstanding his allowed covetous disposition he refused all promised honours and proffered rewards, even of the most extensive kind, to induce him to act contrary to the declared will of God. God on this occasion communicated to him some of the most extraordinary prophetic influences ever conferred on man, Clarke says, and his prophecies are upon the whole clear and pointed, and have been fulfilled in the most remarkable manner, and furnish a very strong argument in proof of divine revelation. Notwithstanding the wicked counsel given to the Midianites, on which account he probably lost his life, the badness of this man's character has been very far overrated, Clarke says, and it does not appear that he was either a hypocrite, false prophet, or a sorcerer in the common acceptation of the term, and he risked even life itself in following and fulfilling the will of the Lord. Though it is expressly asserted that Israel's committing whoredom with the daughters of Moab was brought about by the evil counsel given by Balaam, yet it does not appear from the text that he had those most criminal intentions which are generally attributed to him, Clarke says; he would therefore simply say that the counsel given by Balaam to Balak might have been to form alliances with this people, especially through the medium of matrimonial connections, and, seeing they could not conquer them, to endeavour to make them their friends. Though this might not be designed by Balaam to bring them into a snare, yet it was a bad doctrine, as it led to the corruption of the holy seed and to an unequal yoking with unbelievers, Clarke says; and it was the Moabitish women, not Balaam, that called the people to the sacrifice of their gods, so that it argued great degeneracy and iniquity in the hearts of the people, on so slight an invitation, to join so suddenly so impure a worship and so speedily to cast off the whole form of godliness, with every portion of the fear of the Almighty; therefore the high blame rests ultimately with themselves. John Wesley says the Hebrew Kain means the Kenite, so called either by a transposition of letters, which is very usual in the Hebrew tongue, or from the name of some eminent place where they lived, or person from whom they were descended, though now the memory of them be utterly lost, as it hath fared with innumerable other places and persons famous in their generations and mentioned in ancient heathen writers. Shall be wasted means shall be by degrees diminished by the incursions of divers enemies, till at last the Assyrian comes to complete the work and carries them into captivity, Wesley says, for the Kenites who lived partly among the ten tribes and partly with the two tribes were carried captive with them, part by Salmaneser the King of Assyria and part by Nebuchadnezzar, who also is called an Assyrian. On who shall live, Wesley asks how calamitous and miserable the state of the world will be when the Assyrian, and after him the Chaldean, shall overturn all these parts of the world, and who will be able to keep his heart from fainting under such grievous pressures, and how few will escape the destroying sword. Chittim is a place or people so called from Chittim the son of Javan, whose posterity were very numerous and were first seated in the lesser Asia, and from thence sent forth colonies into the islands of the Aegean sea and into Cyprus, afterwards into Macedonia and other parts of Greece, and then into Italy, Wesley says; whence it comes to pass that by this name is understood sometimes Macedonia, sometimes Italy, and sometimes both, as in this place. Although the Assyrian and Chaldean empire was subdued by the Medes and Persians, yet the chief afflictions of that people came from two hands, both beyond the sea and brought to them by ships, first from the Grecians under Alexander and his successors, then from the Romans, who subdued all the Grecian empire, Wesley says. Eber means the posterity of Eber, the Hebrews, who were the chief and flower of Eber's children, Wesley says; and he also means not the Hebrews, for they shall have a better end and all Israel shall be saved, but the afflicter or scourge of Ashur and Eber, namely the Grecian and Roman empire. Thus Balaam, instead of cursing the church, curses Amalek, the first, and Rome, the last enemy of it, Wesley concludes. To his place means to Mesopotamia, though afterwards he returned to the Midianites and gave them that devilish counsel which was put in practice.

Charles Ellicott says that when God doeth this may be rendered, since or from the time that God sets or determines it, following the Vulgate, or because God determines this. The Chittim, or Kittim, are said to have migrated from Phoenicia to Cyprus and there founded the city of Citium, the modern Chitti, Ellicott says, citing Josephus; the name probably applies to the islands and coasts of the Mediterranean generally, the rendering of the Vulgate being that they shall come in triremes from Italy, and in the parallel passage in Daniel, which is obviously founded upon this verse, the Vulgate identifies the Kittim with the Romans. Some understand by Eber the Hebrews only, Ellicott says; the word, however, appears to be used in a wider signification, as comprising all the children of Eber, and perhaps the word Asshur may here be used to denote the Eastern Shemites and Eber the Western Shemites. And he also shall perish for ever refers to the victorious power which was to afflict Asshur and Eber, Ellicott says, and he quotes Keil, that the overthrow of this last power of the world, concerning which the prophet Daniel was the first to receive and proclaim new revelations, belongs to the end of the days, in which the star out of Jacob is to rise upon Israel as a bright morning-star. There is no evidence as to the manner in which Balaam's prophecies came into the hands of the Israelites, Ellicott adds: it is possible that he may have communicated them to Moses, in the expectation of receiving from him the reward which he had failed to obtain from Balak, or, if captured, in the hope of thereby saving his life. And returned to his place: Balaam probably set out with the intention of returning home, Ellicott says, but the sequel shows that he remained amongst the Midianites and perished with them. Keil and Delitzsch say the fourth saying applies to Asshur and is introduced by an exclamation of woe: who will live, when God sets this, and ships come from the side of Chittim, and press Asshur, and press Eber, and he also perishes. The words woe, who will live, point to the fearfulness of the following judgment, which went deep to the heart of the seer because it would fall upon the sons of his own people, Keil says; the meaning is, in Hengstenberg's words, who will preserve his life in the universal catastrophe that is coming. The phrase means either since the setting of it, equivalent to from the time when God sets or determines this, or on account of the setting of it, that is, because God determines this, Keil says, the verb being applied to that which God establishes, ordains or brings to pass. At the close of this announcement Balaam and Balak departed from one another, Keil says: Balaam rose up and went and turned towards his place, that is, set out on the way to his house, and king Balak also went his way. The Hebrew does not mean he returned to his place, into his home beyond the Euphrates, but merely he turned towards his place, Keil says; that he really returned home is not implied in the words themselves, and the question whether he did so must be determined from other circumstances, for in the further course of the history we learn that Balaam went to the Midianites and advised them to seduce the Israelites to unfaithfulness to Jehovah.

debates: How the clause about Asshur should be construed: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all take it historically of the Kenites being swept up in the Assyrian and Babylonian deportations, Clarke finding confirmation in Kenites appearing among the returned exiles; Calvin calls it harsh and unnatural to apply the clause to the Kenites at all, reports that most refer it to Israel but divide between an affirmative and an interrogative rendering, and prefers the interrogative, how long shall Asshur hold thee captive, since the point is that the promised prosperity would be mixed with heavy affliction

Who Eber is: Wesley takes it of the Hebrews, the chief and flower of Eber's children, and carefully excludes them from the he also who perishes, since all Israel shall be saved; Ellicott keeps the Hebrews but widens the word to all the children of Eber, and conjectures that Asshur may stand for the Eastern and Eber for the Western Shemites; Clarke excludes the Hebrews altogether and derives the name from the verb to pass over, taking it of the peoples beyond the Euphrates whom Alexander destroyed

Whether Chittim means Greece or Rome: Clarke reports the two views and Calmet's strong contention for Macedonia, then follows Ainsworth in allowing both; Calvin says the name is used generally of Greece but is transferred to Italy, and that both the Greeks under Alexander and the Romans after them are meant; Gill reaches the same conclusion by way of the Targums, one reading Italy and the other the Roman legions; Wesley says the name means sometimes one, sometimes the other, and here both; Ellicott notes that the Vulgate renders it triremes from Italy and identifies the Kittim with the Romans in Daniel

How far Balaam is to be blamed: Clarke argues in seventeen numbered propositions that the badness of this man's character has been very far overrated, that he was neither hypocrite nor false prophet nor sorcerer in the common sense, that covetousness is almost the only blot on him, and that his fatal counsel may have been no more than advice to seek alliance by marriage with a people Moab could not conquer, the blame for what followed resting ultimately on Israel; this stands against the reading of Balaam maintained through the rest of the chapter
